cross_tool_domains.attrition: High concern / Serious risk: Although all 53 municipalities are retained in the narrative property-tax totals, 1 municipality (Aranzazu) is dropped from SGP transfer analyses, 20 of 53 municipalities are absent from water and sewerage subscriber/coverage analyses (15 due to pre-2008 cadastral update timing relative to SUI data availability and 5—Marmato, Norcasia, Pensilvania, Pueblo Rico and Córdoba—due to missing SUI data, with several remaining municipalities truncated to 4-year windows), and 11 of 53 municipalities are excluded from IRCA water-quality analyses (Aranzazu plus 10 municipalities missing SIVICAP/IRCA observations). Missingness in municipal utility and sanitary reporting is plausibly correlated with local institutional capacity.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Critical risk: The design relies exclusively on municipality-by-municipality univariate paired t-tests comparing 5-year pre-update and 5-year post-update periods (trimmed means with df = 2 or 3) without a contemporaneous control group, panel fixed effects, inflation deflation, or covariate adjustment. Secular time trends, nominal price growth, urbanization dynamics, national transfer formulas (Ley 1176 de 2007; indigenous reserve allocations), and concurrent municipal fiscal strategies (tax statute reforms under Ley 1450 de 2011, arrears recovery drives, early-payment incentives) are completely confounded with cadastral updating.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate concern: Cadastral update years are drawn from official IGAC (2020) administrative records anchored to the statutory 5-year update mandate (Ley 1450 de 2011, Art. 24), and statutory SGP rules (Constitución Arts. 356–357, Ley 715, Decreto 416 de 2007, Ley 1176 de 2007) are accurately cited. However, exposure operationalization treats cadastral updating as a binary municipal event despite asynchronous urban-only or rural-only updates in 6 municipalities (e.g., La Tebaida, Circasia, Montenegro, Génova, Pijao, Pueblo Rico), includes the update year itself inside Period 1 without verifying fiscal effective dates, and does not measure parallel municipal tax-code or collection reforms.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Serious risk: While data come from official national repositories (IGAC, DNP-OEC/TerriData/SICODIS, SSPD-SUI, INS-SIVICAP), severe measurement artifacts affect the outcomes: (1) 20 of 33 analyzed municipalities had anomalous outlier values in SUI water/sewerage subscriber reports (Footnote 3); (2) aqueduct and sewerage coverage were approximated via an author-constructed proxy dividing SUI subscribers by IGAC cadastral parcels, mechanically coupling the denominator to the cadastral update intervention itself (and yielding -Inf t-statistics and NaN effect sizes in Table 6); (3) IRCA changes reflect varying annual sanitary sampling frequency alongside water contamination; and (4) 2000–2020 monetary series (property tax and SGP transfers) have no reported inflation adjustment.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / Serious concern: Water and sewerage coverage were not taken from verified household access surveys or consistent official coverage series, but from an improvised proxy ratio of SUI subscribers to cadastral parcels (whose formula image on PDF p. 7 is not rendered in text and whose denominator shifts with cadastral updating), unable to disaggregate urban vs. rural service areas. SUI subscriber counts suffered from documented reporting outliers in 20 municipalities, and INS-SIVICAP IRCA water-quality scores suffered from inconsistent annual sample counts and missing municipal series.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern (no pre-analysis plan): No pre-registration or protocol exists. While the author transparently reports null findings across outcomes and candidly discusses SUI outliers and confounding mechanisms, Tables 2, 3 and 4 truncate printed rows at 42 municipalities despite the text reporting analyses of 53 (Tables 2–3) and 52 (Table 4) municipalities, Table 7 prints 41 rows instead of the stated 42 (and omits a significance asterisk on Palestina at p = 0.042), and stated observation year ranges vary inconsistently across p. 103, p. 112 and p. 113. Conducting roughly 300 unadjusted municipality-level tests at alpha = 0.05 also inflates family-wise Type I error.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate risk: The target universe covers the complete census of 53 municipalities in Caldas, Quindío and Risaralda, avoiding arbitrary convenience sampling at the study-entry stage. However, conditioning inclusion in the water/sewerage (n = 33) and IRCA (n = 42) sub-analyses on calendar-year overlap between municipal cadastral update dates (2006/2008 onward) and national platform data availability systematically excludes earlier-updating and data-poor municipalities.

domain_ratings.justification: Each municipality is evaluated via an uncontrolled before-and-after Robust Paired Samples T-Test comparing 5 pre-update years against 5 post-update years (df = 2 or 3 after trimming), with zero control units and zero adjustment for secular time trends, inflation, demographic/urban growth, or concurrent fiscal/regulatory factors. The author explicitly notes that tax increases also reflected municipal tax-code adjustments under Ley 1450 de 2011, arrears collection, and prompt-payment discounts (p. 107), SGP shifts reflected indigenous reserve criteria (p. 107), subscriber increases reflected urban growth dynamics (p. 112), and IRCA shifts reflected changes in sanitary sample counts or source pollution (p. 112). Under ROBINS-I, unadjusted secular trends in an uncontrolled pre-post design constitute Critical confounding risk.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6–8, 11, 16–17 (pp. 102–104, 107, 112–113; Metodología y Datos, Resultados, Conclusiones)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: The overarching frame includes all 53 municipalities in Caldas, Quindío and Risaralda, and follow-up windows are defined symmetrically around each municipality's cadastral update year (Period 1 vs. Period 2). However, eligibility for the water/sewerage (updating from 2008 onward) and IRCA (updating from 2006/2011 onward) analyses was conditioned on when a municipality updated its cadastre relative to SUI (from 2005) and INS (from 2007) database availability, excluding early-updating municipalities from service-delivery evaluations.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 7–8, 11, 16 (pp. 103–104, 107, 112; Metodología y Datos, Figura 1, Tabla 1, Resultados)

domain_ratings.justification: Intervention timing (year of cadastral update) is obtained from official IGAC (2020) records prior to post-period outcomes. However, in 6 municipalities cadastral updating was asynchronous between urban and rural zones (e.g., urban-only updates in La Tebaida, Circasia, Montenegro, Génova and Pijao; rural-only in Pueblo Rico; p. 104, Tabla 1), yet the intervention is analyzed against municipal-wide fiscal and utility totals because urban and rural subscribers could not be disaggregated (p. 113). Additionally, Period 1 includes the update year itself (e.g., 2004–2008 for a 2008 update) without documenting exact fiscal entry-into-force dates.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6, 8, 17 (pp. 102, 104, 113; Metodología y Datos, Resultados, Tabla 1, Conclusiones)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: Under an observational policy evaluation of cadastral updating, concurrent co-interventions were systematically unbalanced between pre- and post-update windows and unadjusted: municipalities enacted local tax-statute reforms pursuant to Ley 1450 de 2011, arrears recovery campaigns, and taxpayer discount schemes (p. 107, p. 113), while national SGP water/sanitation certification and allocation rules shifted under Decreto 416 de 2007 and Ley 1176 de 2007 (p. 102, p. 107).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6, 11, 17 (pp. 102, 107, 113; Catastro y SGP, Resultados, Conclusiones)

domain_ratings.justification: Substantial municipality-level and year-level exclusions occurred due to missing outcome records: 5 of 38 time-eligible municipalities (Marmato, Norcasia, Pensilvania, Pueblo Rico and Córdoba; 13.2%) were excluded from aqueduct and sewerage analyses, several included municipalities had only 4 years of data instead of 5 (p. 107), 10 of 52 municipalities (19.2%) were excluded from IRCA water-quality analyses due to missing samples (p. 112), and Aranzazu was excluded from SGP and IRCA analyses. Because municipal failure to report to SUI or SIVICAP reflects weaker administrative capacity, missingness is likely informative, and no imputation or sensitivity analysis was performed.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6–7, 11, 14, 16–17 (pp. 102–103, 107, 110, 112–113; Metodología y Datos, Resultados, Tabla 6, Conclusiones)

domain_ratings.justification: Although administrative records prevent subjective assessor bias, outcome measurement suffers from major structural flaws: (1) aqueduct and sewerage coverage were computed via an author-constructed proxy ratio of SUI subscribers to cadastral parcels reported by the update (pp. 102–103), mechanically embedding the cadastral update in the outcome denominator and generating degenerate test statistics (-Inf t-values and NaN Cohen's d in Table 6); (2) Footnote 3 (p. 113) documents anomalous outlier values in SUI subscriber reports across 20 of the 33 analyzed municipalities; (3) IRCA values were sensitive to year-to-year changes in sanitary sampling volume (pp. 112–113); and (4) 2000–2020 fiscal series lack documented inflation adjustment.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6–7, 13–17 (pp. 102–103, 109–113; Metodología y Datos, Tablas 5–7, Conclusiones y Nota 3)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: No pre-analysis plan or study protocol is reported (no information on pre-registration). Although null results are openly reported and interpreted conservatively, concrete reporting discrepancies appear in the published article: Tables 2, 3 and 4 omit the final 10–11 municipalities (stopping at 42 rows despite narrative claims of n = 53 and n = 52), Table 7 prints 41 municipalities rather than the stated 42, narrative non-significance percentages for IRCA shift between p. 112 (71.43%) and p. 113 (69%), stated data windows differ across p. 103, p. 112 and p. 113, and hundreds of separate df = 2 paired t-tests are reported without multiple-testing adjustment.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 7, 9–17 (pp. 103, 105–113; Metodología y Datos, Tablas 2–7, Resultados, Conclusiones)

overall_narrative_summary: Pulgarín-Franco (2024) conducts a longitudinal uncontrolled before-and-after quantitative policy evaluation across the 53 municipalities of Caldas, Quindío and Risaralda (Colombia), testing whether municipal cadastral updates (staggered between 2004 and 2015) altered total and per-capita property tax collection, SGP water/sanitation intergovernmental transfers, aqueduct and sewerage subscribers and proxy coverage, and IRCA drinking-water quality risk over 5-year pre-update versus 5-year post-update windows. Appraised with ROBINS-I, the study is at Critical overall risk of bias. Its primary methodological strength is assembling multi-source official administrative records across a complete regional census of 53 municipalities and transparently reporting predominantly null effects on aqueduct coverage and water quality alongside candid discussion of data limitations. However, internal validity for causal inference is critically compromised by the absence of a control group, panel fixed effects, inflation deflation, or covariate adjustment: running separate municipality-level robust paired t-tests (df = 2 or 3) cannot separate cadastral updating from secular trends, urban growth, national SGP allocation rules (Ley 1176 de 2007), or concurrent municipal tax-code and debt-collection reforms (D1 Critical, D4 Serious). In addition, 20 of 53 municipalities are missing from the water/sewerage analyses and 11 of 53 from the IRCA analyses due to calendar truncation and missing administrative reports (D2 Moderate, D5 Serious); urban-only or rural-only updates in 6 municipalities are conflated with municipal-wide outcomes (D3 Moderate); SUI subscriber series contained outliers in 20 municipalities while the proxy coverage denominator mechanically depended on cadastral parcel counts (D6 Serious); and printed result tables omit 10–11 municipalities relative to text totals without a pre-analysis plan (D7 Moderate).
study_design_identified: Quantitative longitudinal uncontrolled before-and-after (pre-post) policy evaluation across 53 municipalities comparing 5-year pre-update and 5-year post-update administrative windows via municipality-specific robust paired-samples t-tests
where_found_summary: Design, administrative data sources (IGAC, DNP-OEC/TerriData/SICODIS, SSPD-SUI, INS-SIVICAP), proxy coverage description, sample restrictions, and Walrus Robust Paired Samples T-Test procedures are reported in 'Metodología y Datos' on PDF pp. 6–7 (pp. 102–103). Municipality update cohorts and pre/post periods appear in 'Resultados' and Tabla 1 on PDF p. 8 (p. 104), with statistical test outputs in Tablas 2–7 and narrative interpretations on PDF pp. 9–16 (pp. 105–112). Co-interventions, SUI outliers (Footnote 3), IRCA sampling variability, and urban/rural disaggregation limitations are detailed in 'Resultados' (PDF pp. 11, 16; pp. 107, 112) and 'Conclusiones' (PDF p. 17; p. 113).
why_tool_chosen: The study empirically evaluates the longitudinal before-and-after impact of a legal/administrative policy intervention—municipal cadastral updating ('actualización catastral' governed by Ley 1450 de 2011 Art. 24)—on municipal fiscal extraction and water/sanitation outcomes across 53 Colombian municipalities using each municipality's 5-year pre-intervention window as the comparator for its 5-year post-intervention window. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, a multi-unit quantitative non-randomized pre-post evaluation of a policy/administrative intervention maps directly to ROBINS-I (unlike JBI Cross-Sectional, as observations are longitudinal pre/post windows rather than a single cross-section, and unlike single-case narrative histories).
